article.title: EURUSD and USDJPY: two falling quotes, two dollar directions
article.dek: Fed reference rates for October 26-30 show the dollar gaining against the euro and slipping against the yen. The quote convention changes the meaning of the move.
article.search_title: EURUSD vs USDJPY: how to read the dollar's direction
article.meta_description: Fed reference rates for October 26-30 show a stronger dollar against the euro and a weaker one against the yen. Read both pairs alongside Treasury yields.
article.social_hook: EURUSD fell. USDJPY fell. Those October 26-30 Fed reference rates meant a stronger dollar against the euro and a weaker one against the yen.
article.substack_body_markdown:
In the Federal Reserve's November 2 H.10 release, EURUSD fell from 1.1178 to 1.1163 over October 26-30, while USDJPY fell from 157.5800 to 157.4700. Both quotes went down. The dollar strengthened against the euro and weakened against the yen. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_3]]

Capital Chronicle's view is that a dollar thesis needs this two-currency check before it is compared with Treasury yields. The small moves in this five-date window show why a dollar view needs a named currency counterpart. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_3]] [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]]

## Two falling quotes, two dollar directions

EURUSD is quoted in US dollars per euro. When that number falls, one euro buys fewer dollars, so the dollar is stronger against the euro. USDJPY is quoted in yen per dollar. A fall means one dollar buys fewer yen, so the dollar is weaker against the yen. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_3]]

The first chart puts both relationships into currency units per dollar and measures their change from October 26. For the euro, that requires taking the reciprocal of EURUSD; the yen quote already measures what one dollar buys. On this basis, the dollar ended October 30 up 0.13% against the euro and down 0.07% against the yen. The inverted euro rate is calculated from the Fed quote. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_3]]

## Match the yield dates before telling the story

Treasury's nominal 10-year par yield moved from 5.00% to 4.94% over the same October 26-30 window, a six-basis-point decline. It reached 5.05% on October 28. The endpoint fall was not a steady daily decline. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]]

Matching dates make the comparison fairer, but these daily observations are not synchronized intraday prices. They do not establish that Treasury yields caused either currency move. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]] [[SOURCE:SOURCE_3]]

The later Treasury reading was 4.90% on November 4. It is a separate context point: the FX observations compared here still end on October 30. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]] [[SOURCE:SOURCE_3]]

## A yield channel, with a countercase

Capital Chronicle's analysis is conditional. A higher US yield could support the dollar if it makes dollar assets relatively more attractive. A fall in EURUSD alongside a rise in USDJPY would show the dollar strengthening against both currencies. That consistent direction would fit the proposed channel; it would not prove that the yield move caused the currency moves. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]] [[SOURCE:SOURCE_3]]

Euro- or yen-specific policy expectations and demand for safer assets could outweigh the US yield channel. The October 26-30 comparison cannot identify which driver dominated. A split dollar response across the two currencies would challenge an explanation built on one common dollar driver. The October 26-30 endpoint split is already a reason to avoid treating the two pairs as one interchangeable dollar position. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]] [[SOURCE:SOURCE_3]]

## The next check

The Bureau of Labor Statistics schedules the October Employment Situation for November 6 at 8:30 a.m. EST. After the release, first read the observed Treasury yield response, then translate each currency pair into the dollar's direction. The question is whether both currencies support the same dollar interpretation. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_2]] [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]] [[SOURCE:SOURCE_3]]

Analysis, not financial advice. Readers decide whether to trade. Capital Chronicle may hold positions in the markets it covers. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_3]]

visual_editorial_decision.countercase: The observed changes are small and cover only five dated reference observations. Domestic European or Japanese developments, relative short-rate expectations and broader risk demand could outweigh the US 10-year yield channel. Daily date alignment supplies neither synchronized intraday pricing nor a causal or correlation estimate. The comparison cannot establish the current spot market or predict the jobs reaction.
visual_editorial_decision.editorial_thesis: A dollar view needs a currency counterpart. In the Fed's October 26–30 reference observations, both EURUSD and USDJPY fell, but those similar-looking quote moves mean opposite dollar directions: modest dollar strength against the euro and modest dollar weakness against the yen. A six-basis-point fall in the same-date Treasury 10-year yield is context, not an explanation proved by these five observations. The useful forward watch is whether a subsequent US yield move is accompanied by the same dollar direction against both currencies, rather than assuming one dollar trade from one currency pair.
